sections.html: Cherax quadricarinatus, also known as Australian red claw crayfish, has been propagated as edible crayfish in aquaculture for decades and was therefore one of the very first Cherax species available for aquaristics. Males can reach up to 30 cm in length; females remain somewhat smaller.

The 3-5 cm long juveniles, which are beautifully colored in light blue, are usually sold. As they get older, the animals become darker. Adult animals have a length of 10-12 cm.

C. quadricarinatus is one of the species on the early warning list of invasive species that may be banned in Europe in the future, as released animals have been repeatedly observed in Spain. Please never release any animals into the wild. Firstly, this is cruelty to animals and secondly, it is strictly forbidden.

Even though Cherax quadricarinatus is one of the largest species, it is also one of the most peaceful. Selection for keeping in aquaculture has probably contributed to the fact that these crayfish, unlike many other crayfish species, are absolutely compatible even with each other and usually do not even damage each other when they are freshly moulted and still butter soft.

The sexes can be distinguished, as in all Cherax species, by the sexual openings (gonopores) on the walking legs. In females the gonopores are located on the 3rd, in males on the 5th pair of walking legs. This is the best form of sex determination, especially in young animals. In adults it is easier because only males develop the red blisters on the outside of the scissor finger.

The length of the head carapace (cephalothorax) indicates when C. quadricarinatus becomes sexually mature: males at 17 mm and females at 24.5 mm. This corresponds to a total length of approx. 4.5 – 6 cm.
